title: Automated Red-Teaming Coverage Blind Spots: What Attacks Do LLM-Based Red Teams Systematically Miss?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if automated red-teaming systematically misses the most dangerous categories (CBRN, CSAM), it provides false assurance. Identifying blind spots motivates hybrid human-automated pipelines. Clear, actionable finding.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Uses existing frameworks (PAIR, TAP via AISafetyLab) to generate attacks, then categorizes outputs against AILuminate taxonomy. Primarily analysis and categorization work rather than ML training. Guided beginners can execute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable: distribution comparison of automated vs. human attacks across hazard categories. Uses existing tools and benchmarks. Can be scoped to 2 red-team methods and 1 target model. Fits in 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: While limitations of automated red teaming are discussed qualitatively -- automated scans catch 60-70% of vulnerabilities found manually, chained attacks bypass 94% of models that pass isolated checks -- no published work systematically maps the distribution of automated vs. human attack coverage across hazard categories like the AILuminate taxonomy. AutoRedTeamer (ICLR 2025 submission) and SafeSearch (arXiv:2509.23694) advance automated red-teaming capabilities but do not analyze their blind spots by hazard category. The specific empirical comparison of attack category distributions between PAIR/TAP output and human red-team benchmarks is a novel and actionable contribution.
